KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 06 November 2020 

Dr Wang
Saffron Park Hospital

Saffron Park, London, E14 7JL
Dear Dr Wang
John Doe, DOB: 09-02-1941, Hospital No: P546484 NHS No. 5484656746
Flat 15 Roundwood Road, London, E14 7JL 

I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today by video link with the ward team. He is a bedbound older adult residing in a nursing facility, and most of the history was provided by his named nurse and the weekday caregiver, who also maintain a seizure observation log.

The caregiving staff report variability in recent events, noting “one or three seizures last month” depending on which entries were counted as full events versus brief episodes without clear impairment. They describe brief behavioural arrest with unresponsiveness, occasional right arm tremor, and post-event confusion lasting up to 20 minutes. There has been no reported tongue biting or head injury. No clear daytime pattern; some episodes occurred around early morning care. The team deny intercurrent infection, but he has had reduced oral intake on some days.

He is currently on Levetiracetam 750 mg b.d. and Lamotrigine 50 mg b.d., administered crushed with soft food. He has tolerated these without rash or clear mood change. The nurse notes intermittent daytime somnolence and mild dizziness on sitting up, which may be multifactorial given his frailty and concurrent medications for blood pressure and constipation. They also report occasional myoclonic jerks during repositioning, which are not clearly time-linked to the recorded seizures.

Examination today was limited by the remote setting. He was rousable to voice, oriented to person, followed one-step commands inconsistently, with no focal asymmetry appreciated on gross limb movements. No cardiorespiratory distress. Skin intact with pressure-relief measures in place. Most observations were relayed by staff.

Plan:
- Continue current antiepileptic regimen unchanged for now given the nursing team’s report of “one or three seizures last month” and the uncertainty about which events represent definite seizures.
- The facility will maintain a structured seizure diary capturing: exact time, witnessed features (including eye deviation, limb involvement, automatisms), duration, recovery phase, possible triggers (missed doses, sleep disruption, infection), and pre-event observations.
- Arrange serum levels for Lamotrigine and routine bloods (U&E, LFT, FBC) through the nursing facility within the next two weeks to check for metabolic contributors and adherence proxies; ensure results are forwarded to the clinic.
- Request an in-reach community EEG if feasible to help characterise events, acknowledging the limitations in a bedbound patient.
- Nursing advice: maintain strict medication administration times, ensure hydration, and continue pressure-area care. Observe for any new focal deficits or prolonged events (>5 minutes), for which emergency protocols should be followed.
- We will review in 8–10 weeks via telemedicine with the same caregivers present and the updated seizure diary to guide any medication adjustments.

Please let me know if there are changes in his baseline cognition, suspected infection, or if the events escalate in frequency or duration before the planned review.

Yours sincerely

King's College Hospital 

Department of Neurosciences 

Clinic Date: 05 April 2023 

Dr A. Patel
Consultant Neurologist  
King's College Hospital  
Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS  

Dear Dr A. Patel
Consultant Neurologist,  

Daniel Harris, DOB: 14-03-1982, Hospital No: KCH742915 NHS No. 9065183274  
78 Brookfield Road, London, SE15 2LP

Thank you for asking me to review your patient. He attended with his partner and provided a clear diary of recent events. Unfortunately, there is evidence of clinical deterioration over the past month. He reports increased day-to-day difficulty with concentration, intermittent word-finding pauses, and escalating fatigue and irritability that he attributes to his current polytherapy. Adverse effects are becoming bothersome (notably daytime somnolence, unsteadiness on rapid head turns, and blunted mood), yet seizure control remains suboptimal. Over the last week he recorded five focal cognitive and six focal non-motors in last week, occurring at variable times without an obvious precipitant. Several of these were clustered over two consecutive mornings, with prolonged post-event disorientation on one occasion. His partner also notes brief nocturnal arousals with confusion, though no clear witnessed generalised convulsions.

He remains adherent to medication and has not missed doses; he denies alcohol or illicit substance use. Sleep has been fragmented, in part due to early-morning awakenings. He is using a smartphone seizure diary, and we reviewed consistent timestamped entries. There has been no recent intercurrent illness. He has not driven and understands the DVLA guidance as previously discussed.

Examination today was non-focal. Gait was steady on slow turns but he felt light-headed on tandem stepping. No papilloedema. Cardiovascular and systemic review unremarkable. Mood was subdued but there was no thought disorder or psychotic features. 

Investigations to date include a prior routine EEG (last year) that was non-diagnostic and a brain MRI (18 months ago) reported as structurally unremarkable. Given the current pattern and the worsening frequency and impact, I am concerned that, despite polytherapy, control is not adequate and tolerability is poor. We discussed the need to clarify the electroclinical pattern and to consider rationalisation of treatment if safe to do so. He is agreeable to expedited prolonged video-EEG monitoring as an inpatient, and I will request this urgently. I will also arrange updated bloods (FBC, U&E, LFT, bone profile, vitamin D, thyroid function) and drug levels where available to check for toxicity or interactions contributing to the adverse effects.

We reviewed general measures: regular sleep schedule, hydration, and avoidance of missed meals. He and his partner are aware of seizure first aid and have a plan to escalate if events become longer or different in character. I provided contact details for our epilepsy nurse specialist for interim support while we await telemetry. 

I will update you once monitoring is completed and results are available. In the meantime, I have not altered his current regimen today due to the risk of further destabilisation, but the trajectory is concerning, and I anticipate we may need to rationalise therapy soon depending on monitoring findings and tolerability.

Yours sincerely

Epilepsy Centre

Neurosciences Division

From: Dr Emma Clarke (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Sent: 07 September 2021 10:15
To: neuro.epilepsyclinic@nhs.net
Cc: Dr Ravi Shah (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Fiona Ellis (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Subject: Worsening seizure control post-partum

Dear Emma,

Epilepsy Diagnosis:

The patient has generalised epilepsy.

Current Concerns and Context:

Since delivering her baby recently, she reports notable low mood and significant fatigue. She perceives that her seizure control has deteriorated in this post-partum period, and her partner corroborates increased episodes of brief behavioural arrest and sudden drops without warning. Sleep is fragmented due to night feeds, and she feels more anxious about caring for the newborn when alone.

Present Medication:

1. Tegretol Retard 600 mg twice daily
2. Keppra 500 mg twice daily

Present Seizure Frequency:

She reports one drop attacks and seven absence seizures in the past two months. These have clustered around periods of marked sleep deprivation.

Assessment:

The temporal relationship with the post-partum period, compounded by low mood and fatigue, is consistent with her perceived deterioration. There are no intercurrent illnesses or missed doses reported. No clear provoking factors beyond sleep disruption have been identified.

Plan of Action:

- Safety and support: We have discussed practical safety measures for drop attacks, including avoiding carrying the baby on stairs and using seated changing where possible. She will keep a seizure diary noting sleep, mood, and timing of episodes.
- Monitoring: We will arrange a follow-up in eight weeks to review seizure burden, mood, and sleep patterns, and to reassess management once the post-partum routine stabilises.
- Communication: She understands to contact the service promptly if drop attacks increase or injuries occur.

I will keep you updated following her next review.

With best wishes,

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 05 January 2016 

Dr Ahmed
North Thames Medical Centre

114 Wharf Road, London, N1 7GR
Dear Dr Ahmed
Michael Carter, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: NHS847201 NHS No. 7483926159
22B Millbank Court, London, SW1P 3SY 

I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today. He has Combined Generalised and Focal Epilepsy Type, with a history indicating both generalised and focal epilepsy. Since his last review, his condition has been deteriorating. He reports recent events associated with falls and minor injuries, including a bruised shoulder and abrasions to the knees following unwitnessed collapses at home and while commuting. Prior to this deterioration, his seizure frequency was three clusters this month; each ≈four absences in the morning, which he described as brief staring spells with impaired awareness and rapid recovery.

Over the past two months he has experienced one drop attacks and seven convulsions in the past two months. The convulsions have been predominantly generalised tonic–clonic events occurring without clear warning, twice from sleep, with post-ictal confusion lasting up to an hour. In addition, he describes focal onset events with a rising epigastric sensation, brief speech arrest and right-hand automatisms, occurring several times per week, some evolving into generalised convulsions. His partner has noted eyelid fluttering and brief behavioural arrest consistent with generalised absence phenomena on several mornings. He denies tongue-biting but reports occasional urinary incontinence after the longer convulsions.

Medication at present: Lamotrigine 200 mg b.d., Levetiracetam 1 g b.d., and Lacosamide 150 mg b.d. He is adherent by report, using a pill organiser and smartphone reminders. He notes increased tiredness and occasional light-headedness but no rash or mood change. There is no reported alcohol excess; sleep has been fragmented due to nocturnal events. He remains employed but has missed shifts due to recovery days after convulsions. He does not drive.

Neurological examination today was non-focal. Cardiovascular observations were stable. There is mild tenderness over the right deltoid consistent with recent soft-tissue injury. We reviewed seizure first aid, injury precautions, and safety around bathing and heights. Given the clear increase in event burden and the emergence of drop attacks with injury, I have arranged an expedited video-EEG telemetry admission and an updated MRI brain with epilepsy protocol. I have also requested serum antiepileptic drug levels (where applicable), U&E, LFT, FBC, and vitamin D. We discussed interim strategies including ensuring adequate sleep, stress management, and consistent medication timing. 

I will revisit his regimen once we have the telemetry and imaging data, as the mixed semiologies support his known diagnosis of combined generalised and focal epilepsy, and treatment adjustment may be needed. I have provided him with an emergency care plan and advised his employer regarding phased duties to reduce risk pending further evaluation.

Yours sincerely

University College Hospital

Clinic Date: 20 November 2021

Dr Susan
University College Hospital
National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, London WC1N 3BG

Dear Dr Susan,

William Harris, DOB: 15-02-1965, Hospital No: H563829 NHS No. 9273645810
10 Meadow Park, London, EC1V 9BT

Summary/Diagnoses: Focal epilepsy with impaired awareness; history of traumatic brain injury; travel-related anxiety; osteoporosis; former alcohol dependence (in sustained remission); hypertension; hyperlipidaemia. Currently residing in supported accommodation. Smoker.

Medication: Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily; Carbamazepine (Tegretol Retard) 400 mg twice daily; Topiramate 75 mg morning and 100 mg evening; Atorvastatin 20 mg once daily; Lansoprazole 30 mg once daily; Bisoprolol 5 mg once daily; Ramipril 5 mg once daily; Thiamine 100 mg once daily; Vitamin B compound strong one tablet daily; Calcium/Vitamin D supplements; Carbocisteine 750 mg twice daily; Emollients as required.

I reviewed Bill in clinic today, accompanied by his key worker from the residence. He remains engaged with routines and reports improved appetite. He uses a single-point stick outdoors and is independent indoors. No recent falls. Sleep has improved since a change to a quieter room. He continues to abstain from alcohol and attends weekly wellbeing sessions.

Focal epilepsy: Bill describes stereotyped focal impaired-awareness episodes featuring a rising epigastric sensation, brief arrest of speech, right facial pulling, and post-event confusion for several minutes. Importantly, he and staff document 5 or 7 focal onset seizures in three weeks during a recent period that included an episode while travelling by air. He links this cluster to marked anticipatory and in-flight anxiety, sleep disruption the night before travel, and missed hydration. Outside that three‑week window, there have been no further episodes for the last six weeks. There has been no secondary generalisation, tongue biting, or injuries. No clear intercurrent infection. Medication adherence is generally good; one evening dose of levetiracetam may have been late on the day of outbound travel.

Travel context: Bill acknowledges travel anxiety, particularly around security checks and take-off. He is open to structured preparation and timing medication around flight schedules. No panic attacks outside travel.

Examination: Afebrile, BP 132/78 mmHg, pulse 66 bpm regular. Neurological exam unchanged: mild increased tone right upper limb, subtle right pronator drift, gait slightly wide-based but safe with stick. No focal tenderness; feet intact, no callosities today. Cognition stable to brief screening; orientation preserved.

Plan:
- Diagnosis reaffirmed as focal epilepsy. Maintain current anti-seizure regimen without dose change, given six seizure-free weeks following the travel-related cluster.
- Provide a written travel plan: ensure adherence with doses timed to flight schedule, maintain sleep the night before, regular hydration, and avoidance of excess caffeine. Airport letter supplied to carry medicines in hand luggage.
- Offer brief anxiety management strategies and signpost to primary care for short-term psychological support focused on travel anxiety.
- Safety advice reinforced: no swimming unsupervised, avoid heights, and comply with DVLA guidance—he is not driving.
- Bloods: request U&E, LFT, FBC, vitamin D, and carbamazepine level via practice in the next two weeks.
- Bone health: continue calcium/vitamin D; DEXA recheck due next year.
- Follow-up: neurology clinic in 6 months, sooner if further clusters or any generalised tonic-clonic seizure.

Yours sincerely,

Dr Kate

Dear Dr Kate
Elliot Carter, DOB: 14-03-1991, Hospital No: K593012 NHS No. 7712048891
12 Willow Bank, Newcastle-under-Lyme, ST5 3PA

Diagnoses/summary: Generalised epilepsy with predominantly nocturnal events as per partner reports; partner was not present at today’s review. Historic EEG reportedly demonstrated generalised spike–wave activity; prior MRI (2018) reported as structurally normal. No known learning disability. No history of febrile convulsions. No family history of epilepsy volunteered.

Current seizure pattern and history: The patient describes disrupted sleep and unrefreshing mornings, with tongue soreness on two occasions and bedclothes disarray. Although the partner was not present today, prior collateral history has suggested night-time events. Over the past two months, the patient reports three focal onset seizures and three focal automatisms in the past two months, occurring in the context of otherwise predominantly nocturnal generalised events. Daytime awareness lapses have been brief without injury. No reported status epilepticus. No clear catamenial pattern. Alcohol intake minimal; no recreational drugs.

Medication history: Currently on Sodium Valproate 500 mg twice daily (started 2020, partial response, weight gain), and Levetiracetam 1 g twice daily (added 2022, mood irritability but acceptable). Rescue: Buccal midazolam held at home—unused in the past year. Previously tried and stopped due to side effects or inefficacy: Lamotrigine (rash), Topiramate (cognitive slowing, paresthesia), Zonisamide (poor appetite), Clobazam (sedation). No known medication allergies.

Relevant comorbidities: Mild asthma (inhaled beclometasone as needed). Migraine without aura approximately monthly. No known cardiac disease. Last vitamin D low–normal (2024). Driving: not driving and aware of DVLA guidance.

Interim history since last review: Sleep schedule irregular due to shift work. Stress at work reported. No recent infections. Reports adherence to medication with occasional late evening doses. Has begun keeping a diary; smartwatch data suggests nocturnal movement clusters twice weekly.

Examination today: Well-appearing, oriented, normal speech, no focal neurological deficits. Weight stable over the past year. Blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm regular.

Investigations: Repeat serum valproate level to be checked (trough). U&E, LFTs, FBC requested. Consider repeat EEG with sleep deprivation to capture generalised discharges and nocturnal events; ambulatory EEG if scheduling delays.

Plan:
- Generalised epilepsy: Given ongoing nocturnal events and the pattern over the past two months (three focal onset seizures and three focal automatisms in the past two months alongside suspected generalised events), we will prioritise sleep optimisation and adherence. No immediate drug changes today pending bloods and EEG.
- Medication optimisation: If trough valproate level subtherapeutic, consider incremental increase to target range with monitoring of LFTs and weight. If levels therapeutic yet events persist, discuss swap from Levetiracetam to Brivaracetam for mood tolerability, or consideration of Perampanel as adjunct, balancing side-effect profile. The patient understands this staged approach.
- Safety: Night-time precautions discussed (low bed height, remove sharp furniture edges, partner to use side positioning if safe, consider bed alarm). Buccal midazolam supply to be checked in date. Seizure diary to continue.
- Lifestyle: Advice on regular sleep routine despite shifts; sleep hygiene leaflet provided. Limit alcohol. Encourage vitamin D supplementation and weight maintenance.
- DVLA: Patient is not driving and will continue to follow DVLA regulations for epilepsy.
- Follow-up: Nurse telephone check-in in 6 weeks to review seizure diary, sleep schedule, and blood results. Clinic review in 4 months, earlier if events escalate or injuries occur.

Thank you for your ongoing care. Please let me know if there are concerns or if workplace adjustments for stable shifts are feasible.

Yours sincerely

Dr Sarah Ahmed
Saffron Park Hospital

Saffron Park, London, E14 7JL
Dear Dr Sarah Ahmed
Michael Carter, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: M837462 NHS No. 7845129630
12B Haverstock Close, London, E14 2PQ 

I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today. He describes recurring episodes since adolescence with preserved awareness in some events and collapse with shaking in others, but with variable semiology and no consistent focal features reported by witnesses. He has a remote history of mild traumatic brain injury in his early 20s without documented loss of consciousness beyond a few minutes and no neurosurgical intervention. 

Since his last community review six months ago, he reports clusters of brief warning sensations (described as a rising internal feeling and metallic taste) on some days, and a smaller number of longer events with loss of awareness. He estimates the more disruptive events occur q2 - 3wk, often later in the evening, sometimes after poor sleep. There is no consistent relation to alcohol intake, and he does not drive. Post-event confusion lasts 10–20 minutes, with fatigue into the following day. There have been no tongue bites or significant injuries in the last year, though he notes occasional myalgia afterwards. Family videos are inconclusive due to partial view and low light. 

Medication at present: Levetiracetam 1000 mg b.d. and Lamotrigine 150 mg b.d. He has tolerated these with intermittent irritability (patient-reported) and mild sleep fragmentation; no rash, no gastrointestinal upset. Adherence is reported as good, supported by pharmacy refill records. He uses a phone reminder system for dosing. There is no history of status episodes or emergency department presentations in the past 12 months. 

Examination today was unremarkable with no lateralising neurological signs. Routine bloods last month (FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, vitamin D) were within reference limits. An MRI brain (3T epilepsy protocol) performed in 2023 was reported as structurally normal without mesial temporal sclerosis, focal cortical dysplasia, or microhaemorrhage. Interictal EEG in 2022 showed rare non-specific slowing without epileptiform discharges. 

Plan: Given the reported frequency of more disruptive events at approximately q2 - 3wk and the historical variability in semiology, I have arranged ambulatory EEG with home video capture to improve event-characterisation. I have also requested retrieval of prior imaging for re-review at the neuroradiology meeting in case of subtle sequelae of the remote mild traumatic brain injury. For now, I have not altered medication pending these results. We discussed sleep hygiene, stress management strategies (patient-led), and the value of witness recordings when safe. He is aware of safety precautions regarding bathing, cooking with open flames, and working at heights. 

I will see him again in three months or sooner if the ambulatory EEG captures typical events earlier. He knows to contact the service if frequency increases beyond the current q2 - 3wk pattern or if new features emerge such as prolonged confusion, focal neurological deficits, or injury. 

Yours sincerely

Diagnoses/summary: Recurrent seizures of uncertain classification; prior EEGs inconclusive; MRI brain (2017) structurally unremarkable. Occupational setting includes prolonged standing and exposure to unpredictable crowd surges at a busy metro station gate line.

Previous medication: Levetiracetam (mood irritability), sodium valproate (weight gain, tremor), carbamazepine (dizziness), lamotrigine (rash), topiramate (word-finding difficulty), lacosamide (no clear benefit), clobazam PRN (sedation). Not previously trialled: perampanel, zonisamide, brivaracetam, pregabalin, tiagabine, rufinamide.

Comorbidities and relevant history: Migraine without aura; occasional orthostatic light-headedness; no known structural cardiac disease; vitamin D insufficiency (treated). No history of febrile convulsions. Family history non-contributory. 

I reviewed Daniel Kerr in clinic today, unaccompanied. Since our last contact in May, he reports that events have been sparse; specifically, he has not noted any further turns for several weeks, including during recent late shifts. He describes continuing prodromal sensations on two occasions (a brief wave of queasiness and metallic taste, each <30 seconds) without progression to a collapse or witnessed convulsion. He has maintained a seizure diary and cross-checked with workplace incident logs; there have been no duty interruptions due to episodes during this interval. He remains vigilant around the gate line during peak passenger flow and wears an ID band. 

Current medication:
- Brivaracetam 50 mg twice daily (initiated June; tolerated)
- Thiamine 100 mg daily
- Vitamin D3 1000 IU daily

Work and safety context: Role involves prolonged standing, exposure to heat during rush hours, and occasional rapid crowd movement. He has arranged, with his manager, access to a staff rest area for brief recovery if prodrome recurs. Hydration is encouraged on shift; he uses a small belt pouch water bottle. Manual handling of barrier gates is shared with colleagues during peak surges. 

Examination today: Alert, oriented; speech fluent; cranial nerves intact; no focal neurological deficits. Cardiovascular exam unremarkable. BMI stable. 

Investigations: No new imaging. Routine bloods in August were within normal limits (U&E, LFT, FBC). Brivaracetam level not routinely monitored. 

Plan:
- Continue brivaracetam 50 mg twice daily for now, given the recent period with essentially no breakthrough events. We discussed that should warning symptoms intensify or if collapses recur, we would consider dose optimisation or an alternative agent (e.g. zonisamide) after risk–benefit review.
- Reinforce workplace measures: avoid missed meals, maintain hydration, and ensure colleagues are aware of his agreed rest protocol during crowd surges. He will continue diary and incident log correlation.
- I have provided a personalised "what to do" card for colleagues regarding first aid for a possible seizure on the concourse (avoid restraint, clear space, time the episode, recovery position if needed). 
- DVLA guidance was reviewed today as per current standards; he confirms he is not driving. 
- Follow-up in 4 months, sooner if any deterioration or if he experiences a loss of awareness or collapse. He will contact the epilepsy nurse specialist line if prodromes become more frequent. 

Side effects and risks were reviewed, including somnolence and mood changes with brivaracetam. He has not noted aggression or mood lability since initiation. We discussed sleep hygiene and migraine triggers. 

Please let me know if there are any issues from your side. Thank you for your ongoing care.

Yours sincerely

I saw James Morton in clinic today accompanied by his sister, who helps organise prescriptions. Since our previous appointment six months ago, there have been no emergency attendances. He reports improved routine with pill dosing after moving to a weekly blister pack, though he and his sister describe occasional delays obtaining medication when the pharmacy has been out of stock, echoing the documented past variability in supply.

Seizure history:

5) Seizure diary to be kept; if events exceed baseline again, contact clinic for expedited review.
6) Routine follow-up in 6 months, sooner if frequency worsens or injuries occur.

Yours sincerely,

Department of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 14 June 2015 

Dr Amelia Patel  
St George’s Hospital  
Department of Neurology, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT  

Dear Dr Amelia Patel,  

Michael Turner, DOB: 22-03-1988, Hospital No: H473920 NHS No. 9938475612  
18 Willow Lane, Wimbledon, London SW19 2PA 

Diagnoses:  

Two unprovoked seizures under evaluation; EEG pending (booked July 2015).  

Current Medication:  

No regular antiepileptic medication at present. PRN buccal midazolam not prescribed.  

Plan:  

- Arrange routine EEG and brain MRI with epilepsy protocol.  
- Provide written seizure first-aid and SUDEP risk counselling.  
- Discuss driving regulations and notify DVLA as appropriate.  
- Review in clinic after investigations; earlier if further events occur.  
- Liaise with community pharmacy regarding continuity of supply if treatment is initiated.  

I reviewed Michael Turner in clinic today following two recent events suggestive of seizures. The first seizure was reported in April 2015 while visiting relatives in Canada. It happened during an afternoon nap, with an unusual tingling spreading from the right hand to the shoulder. The second event took place in June 2015 in the USA, again from sleep, lasting approximately five minutes, with comparable symptoms. There was no clear precipitant identified. There is no personal history of significant head injury, CNS infection, or febrile convulsions. Family history is non-contributory by the patient’s account. Alcohol intake is modest and there is no recreational drug use reported. Sleep had been irregular around the times of travel.  

Past variability in pharmacy supply is documented in the records from previous long-term prescriptions for non-neurological conditions; the patient reports that adherence was impacted at times when pharmacies substituted brands or experienced stock interruptions. We discussed the importance of consistency of supply should an antiseizure medicine be commenced, and I will ensure any future prescription specifies brand consistency and that the community pharmacy is briefed to minimise switching.  

On examination today, general and neurological examinations were normal. Observations were stable. There are no lateralising signs.  

Given the limited number of events, absence of ongoing neurological deficit, and pending investigations, we agreed not to start an antiseizure medication today. Should there be any recurrence, especially with evolving features, we will reconsider treatment promptly. The patient has been advised on sleep hygiene, avoidance of sleep deprivation, and to keep a clear record of any further episodes including timing, duration, semiology, and potential triggers.  

I have advised that they must not drive and should follow DVLA guidance for a first unprovoked seizure, with notification to the DVLA; I have provided supporting documentation. Workplace safety and water safety precautions were reviewed. A seizure action plan and emergency guidance have been supplied.  

I will see Michael Turner after the EEG and MRI are completed, or sooner if further events occur. Please let me know if there are questions or if additional information from primary care becomes available.  

With best wishes,

Focal epilepsy, likely left temporal onset, with secondary generalisation risk. 

History and current status: 

I reviewed Emily Rogers in clinic today. She works as a warehouse picker operating between tall racking and narrow aisles, where lifting tasks and the work pace vary by shift. She reports that her typical event begins with a brief rising epigastric sensation and déjà vu lasting 15–30 seconds, occasionally followed by impaired awareness with automatisms and a short post-event confusion. She has not required rescue medication in the past 12 months and there have been no injuries at work. 

Regarding seizure frequency, she describes a fluctuating pattern around her shift rota. On occasions she is seizure-free for 4 consecutive days, followed by a day with multiple events, typically two tonic seizures. She links these cluster days to early-start shifts with higher lifting demand, though she is unsure whether sleep disruption or physical load is the main trigger. There has been no recent change in caffeine or alcohol intake, and she denies intercurrent illness. 

Medication and investigations: 

- Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily. She reports full adherence and no dose omissions during shift changes.

Workplace context and safety: 

She reports narrow-aisle navigation with handheld scanners and intermittent ladder use to shoulder height; powered lifting aids are available for heavier items. She states she avoids working at height and does not operate forklifts. She also indicates that supervisors are aware of her diagnosis and that a colleague can be called promptly if she feels an aura.

- Continue current anti-seizure medications without change.  
- Arrange ambulatory EEG to capture events during a representative workday.  
- Bloods today: lamotrigine and levetiracetam trough levels, U&E, LFT, FBC, vitamin D.

Summary/ Diagnoses: Generalised epilepsy with tonic–clonic seizures/circadian rhythm disruption due to rotating night shifts/mild anxiety symptoms/smoker (5–7 per day). 

Medication: Valproate 500 mg twice daily.  
Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily.  
Vitamin D 1000 IU daily.  
Omeprazole 20 mg once daily.  

I reviewed James in clinic today. He works rotating shifts, including nights every other week, and reports significant disruption to sleep patterns. He describes fragmented sleep on night rotas and excessive daytime fatigue on the subsequent transition back to days. He denies alcohol misuse. Appetite is stable and weight unchanged. He continues to smoke a few cigarettes daily and is considering nicotine replacement; he will discuss cessation options with his GP. 

Seizures: James has generalised epilepsy. He keeps an electronic diary linked to his phone; however, the past three months include several entries without times due to night duties. He and his partner report two definite generalised tonic–clonic seizures in the last six months (one in May during a post‑night shift morning, one in August on a transition week). He changed from valproate EC tablets to identical dose chrono formulation via pharmacy supply in late April. Since that switch, he feels the pattern has shifted, but it is not clear whether events are more or less frequent overall, given inconsistent recording around night shifts. No myoclonic jerks on awakening have been noted recently. No injuries, tongue-bites on both events, brief post‑ictal confusion 20–30 minutes. No absence episodes witnessed at work. 

Examination: Alert and orientated. Speech normal. Cranial nerves intact. Motor bulk and tone normal, power 5/5 throughout, reflexes symmetric, plantar flexor. Gait steady. No focal neurological deficit. 

Investigations: Last AEeg (2023) showed generalised spike–wave discharges. MRI brain (2022) normal. Routine bloods Dec 2024 normal including LFTs; vitamin D borderline low at that time (on supplementation). 

Plan:  
- Generalised epilepsy: continue current doses of valproate and lamotrigine; no immediate change today given infrequent GTCs and uncertainty around recent frequency after formulation change.  
- Provide a structured seizure and sleep log (paper and digital template) with emphasis on shift patterns, sleep duration, and exact timing of doses and events.  
- Pharmacy: confirm ongoing supply of the same valproate formulation (chrono) to avoid further variability; community pharmacist to add “do not substitute” note where feasible.  
- Occupational advice: discuss with occupational health about stabilising shift patterns where possible (aim to reduce rapid rotations and consecutive nights).  
- Safety: standard seizure first‑aid reinforced; avoid swimming alone, heights, or operating machinery at times of sleep deprivation. Driving status unchanged per DVLA guidance; he is not currently driving.  
- Bloods: request LFTs, FBC, U&E, vitamin D via practice within the next month.  
- Follow‑up: neurology clinic in 6 months or sooner if clear increase in seizures, particularly if events cluster around formulation issues or night shifts. 

Yours sincerely
